_note: Hardscrabble's people (decision 0340). Drafts: Matt's friend may rewrite any of them. Voices and facts are in docs/regions/hardscrabble.md. Every id starts hs_ so the quests session's files can't collide with these.

lines.text: A stocky man in a leather apron is standing at the patch with his hands behind his back.
You've glued it. With ice. Who taught you to lay stone, a squirrel?
Nobody taught me. It shows, I know.
It shows from the road.
That's the Ames line I'm mending. Ameses went west twenty years back.
Then who is it for?
A wall's a promise. You don't stop keeping it because the other fellow moved away.
Been up the hill to look at that stone twice. Still Thayer work.
There's a white stag up at the pound. It wants to go home through the ring wall, and it can't.
Through Coyle's wall? Nothing goes through that. That's what's wrong with it.
Fence man told me to keep off the hill. Hm.
Come and look, at least.
Looking's free.
He picks up his sledge anyway.
You go up together. He stops twice on the Sheep Walk to look at walls, and says nothing about either.
Your patch is where you left it. On the lane. It won't lay itself.
Well. Not properly.
Obed is at the trough with his sledge over his shoulder and a sack at his feet.
Somebody else up the road's been mending badly. I'd like a look at it.
Some of it may have been me.
Then I'll know the work.
Village says I talk to the stones.
Do you?
They don't interrupt. Phebe did. She was usually right.
My boy went up the road. Furnace work. Iron.
Is he good at it?
He'd better be.
I'll stand in front. That's where the weight goes.
Boots matter. Everything else is weather.
Sixty-one winters. I'll get up when I'm ready.
You cast like a man in a hurry. Nobody's chasing you.
The goose and I have an understanding. She keeps off my stones.
Fair coat. Somebody stitched that who meant it.
Good morning. Abner Coyle. I buy for the land company, if you've a farm to sell.
Not here, I'm afraid.
Nobody has, here. They've gone. That's why I'm buying.
Sheep on the hills, three hundred head by spring. It'll be the first thing that's paid in this valley in twenty years.
I rebuilt the stretch on Hobble Hill myself. Dead straight. Mortared. A proper footing. Best wall I've ever put up.
I heard it cracked.
In a week. I don't understand it. I measured everything twice.
Mr. Thayer calls me the fence man. I don't think he means it kindly.
I mean everything kindly. It doesn't seem to help.
We had a farm, when I was small. It went to the bank the year I was nine.
The bank didn't want it either. They let the roof go and sold the wall stones for a road.
So you buy them first.
Somebody ought to want them.
I write everything down. Acres, rods, head of sheep. If it's in the ledger, it happened.
And if it isn't?
Then I haven't got to it yet.
Mr. Thayer took my wall down. All of it, in an afternoon.
And laid his own.
It's crooked, and there's a hole in it. And the frost has stopped.
I've written that down. I don't know what else to do with it.
I keep measuring the gap. A hand, near enough. Facing north. It doesn't get any wider.
Come in, come in. Last shop open. Everybody leaving needs boots.
I'm not leaving. Only passing through.
Same boots.
Stand still. Left foot. Eleven knots and a bit. You've come off the upland road, by that heel, and you don't stop for weather.
There's a pair on the bench near enough your size. No coin, mind. Nobody up here has any. I take goods.
Eleven and a bit, back again. Come to look at the bench?
How are they wearing? Don't tell me. I can see by the heel.
Boots on the bench, stones in the tin. Good boots take a while. Bad ones take longer, because you come back.
I'll be here. Somebody has to be.
Every family that's gone out of here went in my boots. I keep their lasts on the shelf.
In case they come back?
Feet don't change much. Well. They spread.
The Abbotts' youngest was four when they went. I made hers a size up, so she'd grow into them.
She'll be in them by now, wherever she is.
Obed Thayer, going up the road. I've resoled those boots six times.
They're broken in.
They're broken.
Mind the hem. That's the Shattucks' coat. Or will be.
You sew in the meetinghouse?
Best light in town. Nobody minds. Nobody's left to mind.
I let things out, take things in. And I'll sew a charm into a coat or a boot, for the road. My mother did.
Bring me a plain piece and some small thing that's been somewhere. One charm to a piece. The fancy work's for Harlow Bridge.
Let's see it, then. Hold still. Not you. The coat.
Put it on the table. And tell Obed Thayer to stop looking at my seams like that.

tailor.finer: Not that one. That's {tier}. It wants finer hands than mine. Harlow Bridge.

lines.text: Everything I sew into a coat is something to bring a person home. A nail out of the doorframe. Ash from their own hearth.
Has it ever worked?
Nobody's come home yet.
I keep sewing it in.
Obed. You're going, then.
Up the road a way.
I'll let your coat out.
It doesn't need letting out.
It will. You'll eat on the road. Nobody's cooked for you in two years.
We're going down to the mills. Lucy's sister is there. Good wages, she writes.
When do you go?
When it's loaded.
It was loaded Tuesday.
Churn's back in the house. My mother's churn. You don't put a churn on a wagon in the rain.
It isn't raining.
It might.
My father cleared the low field. Eleven years, getting the stones off it. They're in that wall.
They'll still be there.
That's the trouble.
Don't ask him what's on the wagon. Ask him what's come off it.
What's come off it?
The clock. The churn. His father's chair. The chair twice.
I've packed for the mills four times. I could pack it in my sleep. Some nights I do.
My sister writes the mill bell goes at half past four, and everybody gets up for it.
I've got up for cows for twenty years. I don't suppose a bell's any different.
Don't touch the goat. That's the Pikes. The Pikes bite.
The goat is called the Pikes?
The Pikes left her, so she's the Pikes. That's the Dows. That's the Holts. The hens are all the Abbotts.
All of them?
There were a lot of Abbotts.
They're meant to be in the pound. Something's in the pound. It's white and it won't come out and it knocks the wall.
Have you seen it?
Once. It looked at me. Now I'm not allowed up there, and the Holts ate Mama's bonnet.
Mr. Thayer says it went home. Through a hole. On purpose, he says.
So I can have the pound back. Only the Holts won't walk past the wall, and the Holts go first or nobody goes.
Twelve Abbotts, two goats, the Holts, the Merrills and the Lowells. I count them every morning. Most of the Abbotts are in the barn. Mama says the barn isn't a pound.
The Merrills left the horse because he's lame. Mama says they'll send for him.
Will they?
No. I've told him, so he isn't waiting.
When we go, I'm taking all of them.
Are you going?
Papa says next year. He said that last year. I've written it on the barn door so he can't say he didn't.
Mr. Thayer. You're not to spit on my pound.
Wasn't going to.
You spat on the hill wall. Everybody saw.
That's different.
How?
It's how it's done.
The Pikes takes the end of Eldwin's staff in her teeth, thinks about it, and lets go.
The Dows lets Eldwin scratch her ears, then leans on him until he stops.
The Holts grunts and goes on with what used to be a bonnet.
The Merrills rests a back hoof on its toe. He lets Eldwin rub his nose, and goes back to looking at the road.
One of the Abbotts has a look at Eldwin's boot, and finds nothing in it.
The Lowells watches Eldwin from exactly as far away as he is.
Told you we'd get here. Patience did most of it.
Did Obed Thayer take his letter?
Three times I've knocked. Postage due, a dozen eggs, and he says he never asked for any letter.
Is he the one who keeps the walls? The stretch by the Long Wall was laid properly.
That'll be Obed. He walls for nobody. He'll tell you about it.
We'll wait. Patience is good at waiting. Better than me.
Harlow Bridge next, when Patience is ready. She isn't yet.
Forty-two. Mr. Coyle's paid for forty-three. He's very patient about it. Makes it worse.
Forty-three, all in. Mr. Coyle counted them twice and wrote it down.
And you?
Three times. I don't write.
Nice little village. Going cheap.
Is this your house?
It's for sale. I'm keeping an eye on it.
For whom?
Kettle's on.
Your father bought a trowel off me once.
My father never bought anything off anybody.
That's the one.
The Pikes kept a store down the old cut, under the Quarry. Cold keeps leather.
They took the wagon and left the store. Three pairs of my boots in it. One's the boy's.
You want them back?
I want them on the shelf, by the Pikes' last. Nobody's going to wear them. They can sit somewhere.
Mind the cut. It goes further in than the Pikes ever did.
The Pikes' boots.
Toes to the wall. That's Hannah Pike. She always put them away like they'd run off.
He sets them on the shelf beside the Pikes' last, the small pair in front.
There. Now they're somewhere.
For your trouble. And grease your own. They look like a bad week.
The Dows are well. Their boy's gone up two sizes. I said he would.
They asked was the shop still open. I said it's open till it isn't.
Been down the Cut, by the look of your boots.
To the end of it.
Don't go counting the hollows. It's bad for trade, counting.
Tea's stewed. Business isn't. What'll it be?
Quieter up the hill these nights. Bad for trade, quiet. What'll it be?
